newsitem.title: USA: Alcoa sees greater aluminum use in autos.
newsitem.headline: Alcoa sees greater aluminum use in autos.

text.p: Aluminum use is expected to increase in North American vehicles because it will boost fuel economy and cut emissions, Alcoa's Worldwide Automotive Products Director Richard Schultz said.

"Alcoa's goal and the goal of the entire aluminum industry is to lightweight as quickly and efficiently as possible the world's entire automotive fleet," Schultz told an aluminum conference organised by consultants Gorham/Intertech.
Schultz noted that over the last 20 years the aluminum content of cars in North America has gone from 87 pounds per vehicle to 252 pounds per vehicle.

"That is a compound annual growth rate of 5.5 percent," he said. Total U.S. consumption of aluminum in cars and light trucks was about four billion pounds in 1996, and worldwide over 10 billion pounds.
In the last five years, aluminum content was up across the board at Ford Motor Co, Chrysler Corp and General Motors Corp, Schultz said.
He said Ford used the most aluminum in vehicles this year at about 1.2 billion pounds. GM and Chrysler were not far behind at about 1.3 billion and 600 million pounds respectively.

The main uses for aluminum in cars were for power trains, heat exchangers, and wheels. But aluminum is also getting a toehold over steel in steering assemlies, chassis, suspensions, closure panels and bumpers, Schultz said.
"In fact 10 percent of the cars and light trucks produced in North America this year will have at least one aluminum outer body panel," he said.

If growth continues at the same rate over the 20 years, "We will easily reach 750 pounds of aluminum per vehicle in North America by 2015. The minimum we see is 550 pounds per vehicle, and the upside could be 950 pounds."
Every 10 percent reduction in weight brings about a seven percent fuel economy and even greater reductions in emissions, Schultz said.
Aluminum also makes sense for autos because the value of aluminum scrap is 10 times that of steel scrap.
"The retired cars we are bringing back today only contain five percent aluminum, but that aluminum represents 35 to 50 percent of the material scrap value of a car at the end of its useful life."
